chunks: Sa'd narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Musa ibn 'Umar from Musa ibn 'Isa from Marwan ibn Muslim from 'Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about something of forgetfulness (sahw) in the prayer, so he said: 'Shall I not teach you something? If you do it, and then you remember that you completed or fell short, there is no blame upon you.' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'If you are forgetful, build upon what is more likely (the majority). When you have finished and given the salam, stand up and pray what you thought you missed. If you had indeed completed it, there is no blame upon you in this. And if you remember that you had missed something, what you prayed is the completion of what you missed.'

key_terms.السَّهْو: Forgetfulness or lapse of memory during worship
key_terms.الْأَكْثَر: The majority or what is more likely (principle of presumption)

ai.seo_question: How to handle uncertainty about missing parts of the prayer due to forgetfulness?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the principle of 'presumption of continuity' (istishab) in ritual purity and prayer, instructing the worshipper to build upon the most probable state of completion. By performing a compensatory prayer (salat al-nas) after the final salam, the individual resolves doubt without invalidating the initial prayer, reflecting the Shia juristic preference for ease in cases of uncertainty. This method ensures the validity of the obligatory act while addressing the specific gap, demonstrating the practical application of hadith in daily worship.
